Title: Concordance with the MIND diet is associated with lower subsequent epigenetic aging
Authors: Wang, V. H.-C.; Weiss, J.; Gu, Y. Y.; Beasley, J. M.; Johnston, E.; Masurkar, A.; Wronski, D.; Zhang, D. S.
Abstract: Abstract/SummaryHealthy dietary patterns may influence biological aging, but prospective evidence for the Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND) diet is limited. We linked 2013 dietary data to 2016 DNA methylation measures in 1,740 Health and Retirement Study participants. Per 1-s.d. higher MIND score, adjusted differences were -0.4 years for PhenoAge acceleration (95% CI -0.8 to -0.1), -0.3 years for GrimAge acceleration (-0.5 to -0.1) and -0.0054 for methylation Pace of Aging (-0.0098 to -0.0010); all false-discovery-rate q[≤]0.026. Associations persisted after body-mass-index adjustment and selection weighting. Targeted maximum likelihood estimates were concordant with the conventional models, whereas causal forests evaluated in held-out and repeated-split samples found no reproducible evidence that specific subgroups of participants benefited more than others. Greater MIND concordance was associated with lower subsequent epigenetic aging across complementary measures, supporting molecular aging as an intermediate phenotype for diet-aging research.

Title: Who infected the reported cases? Evidence from 678,482 COVID-19 cases with identified infector collected in routine surveillance in the Netherlands, 2020-2022.
Authors: Backer, J. A.; Leung, K. Y.; Andeweg, S. P.; Van de Kassteele, J.; Veldhuijzen, I.; Hahne, S.; Wallinga, J.
Abstract: BackgroundDuring infectious disease outbreaks, characteristics of reported cases are routinely collected. These give information on becoming infected but not on infecting others. We assess whether linking infectees to infectors, together with their characteristics, can help understand transmission.  MethodsFrom the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in the Netherlands, reported cases were asked to identify their most probable infector in routine surveillance, enabling the linking of cases. We assess for the period 27 February 2020 - 11 April 2022 whether the infectees of these transmission pairs are representative of all reported cases, whether the transmission pairs yield verifiable estimates of epidemiological characteristics (here the serial interval), and whether they provide additional information on transmission.  ResultsOf 8,003,008 reported cases, 678,482 (8.5%) could be linked to their most probable infector. These infectees were largely representative of the reported cases regarding age group, sex, and geographical location. The mean serial interval of 3.6 days (sd 3.4 days) from transmission pairs aligns with literature. Transmissions between age groups largely follow known contact patterns. Most transmissions in September 2021 occurred between persons who were not (fully) vaccinated, indicating the effectiveness of the vaccine, and relatively few between persons with different vaccination status, suggesting assortative mixing in vaccination status.  ConclusionTransmission pairs can be efficiently collected in routine surveillance, providing insight into disease transmission. The current post-pandemic period provides an excellent opportunity to adjust reporting systems for linking infectees to their most probable infector as preparation for future outbreaks.

Title: Spatially varying effect estimates of mediation in the presence of spatial auto-correlation
Authors: Hansen, K.; Ma, Y.; Schwartzman, A.; Benmarhnia, T.
Abstract: The use of mediation analysis is common in epidemiology to decompose an exposure-outcome total effect into direct and indirect effects via a given set of mediators. The counterfactual framework in causal inference allowed for great improvements in mediation analysis to define identification assumptions and clarify sources of bias in different settings. Multiple mediation methods have been proposed to consider confounders of various types and for different settings such as longitudinal designs. However, in some settings we may reasonably expect spatially heterogeneous estimates of both natural direct and indirect effects. In various research areas, especially environmental and social epidemiology, we would expect there to be spatial dependence that could be leveraged. In this paper, we describe and compare a set of approaches to perform spatial mediation analyses and conduct an extensive set of simulations to quantify their performance. We also present a case study assessing the spatially heterogeneous mediating role of PM2.5 in the association between income and cardiovascular diseases. We provide all code via GitHub for replication and reproducibility purposes. We find that using a framework combining geographically weighted regression (GWR) and other spatially varying coefficient (SVC) models and the product method of mediation analysis is accurate and precise at estimating spatially heterogeneous effect estimates and handling spatial confounding in a grid setting. Such spatial approaches can be extended to any mediation approach and various confounding structures.

Title: Brownfield land and emergency hospital admissions in England: a small-area ecological study using contamination hazard score as an exposure proxy
Authors: Wang, W.; Konstantinoudis, G.; Beriro, D.; Dack, S.; Davies, B.; Liu, Y.; Kamanyire, R.; Fecht, D.
Abstract: BackgroundEmpirical evidence on the health impacts of brownfield land - previously developed land that may be contaminated - remains limited, mainly due to poorly defined exposures and pathways. Here we assessed associations between an area-level contamination hazard score and emergency hospital admissions across England, using the score as a proxy for the potential contamination associated with brownfield land.  MethodsWe used Lower-layer Super Output Area (LSOA)-level population-weighted contamination hazard scores in Bayesian hierarchical models to examine the risk of emergency hospital admission (age- and sex-standardised, 2010-2019) with a primary diagnosis of i) all causes (excluding external causes), ii) respiratory diseases, and iii) cardiovascular diseases (CVD). Models were adjusted for deprivation, population density, tobacco expenditure, green space, urbanicity, and ethnicity, and included spatially structured and unstructured random effects to account for residual spatial autocorrelation between neighbouring areas. Stratified analyses assessed potential effect modification by deprivation, urban/rural classification, and region.  ResultsWe included 42,875,231 admissions for all natural causes, 6,657,050 for respiratory diseases, and 4,393,461 for CVD across 32,844 LSOAs in England. LSOAs with higher contamination hazard scores showed a non-linear decreasing trend in relative risk (RR) for all health outcomes. Spatial variation was evident, with stronger negative associations in urban and the least deprived LSOAs, while rural and more deprived LSOAs showed weaker associations or greater uncertainty. Region-specific analyses demonstrated inverse associations for all outcomes in London and for all natural causes and respiratory admissions in the North West and East of England. Other regions showed no consistent pattern across outcomes.  ConclusionHigher contamination hazard scores were associated with lower emergency hospital admission risks. This suggests that areas with a greater legacy of potentially contaminating land uses do not necessarily experience poorer contemporary population health. The inverse associations may partly reflect subsequent remediation and urban regeneration, although the underlying mechanisms require further investigation.  HighlightsO_LIA national brownfield study used contamination hazard scores as an exposure proxy. C_LIO_LIHigher contamination hazard scores were linked to lower emergency admission risks. C_LIO_LIInverse associations were strongest in urban areas, least deprived areas and London. C_LIO_LILower risks may reflect redevelopment, not a protective effect of brownfield land. C_LI

Title: Intensive care unit admissions in Germany associated with atmospheric factors: a regional time-series analysis
Authors: Sasse, K.; Merkenschlager, C.; Johler, M.; Baldenius, T.; Droege, P.; Guenster, C.; Ruhnke, T.; Eschrihuela Branz, P.; Proell, L.; Wein, B.; Hettich, S.; Ignatenko, Y.; Oeksuez, T.; Soto-Rey, I.; Hertig, E.
Abstract: IntroductionAtmospheric conditions under climate change constitute an increasing health burden and raise pressure on health care systems. Intensive care units (ICUs) are particularly vulnerable due to their low buffer capacity and high utilization rates. This study aimed to examine the association between atmospheric exposures and ICU admissions for intensive care relevant diseases across Germany.  MethodsWe analyzed daily time-series data on ICU admissions from AOK health insurances and atmospheric data in the period 2009 to 2023. Using principal component analysis, we clustered Germany into eleven human-bioclimatic regions. For each atmospheric predictor, the optimal time lag was selected, and disease-specific predictor sets were defined while accounting for multiple testing. In each region, we fitted quasi-Poisson generalized additive models to estimate disease-specific ICU admission risks associated with atmospheric exposures. Models were stratified by age (<60, [≥]60 years) and sex. Model performance was assessed using (weighted) explained deviance (WED).  ResultsOver the 15-year study period, on average 2,526 ICU admissions per 100,000 AOK insured persons per year were recorded in Germany (44% women, 74.3% aged [≥]60 years). Pressure-related variables were most frequently associated with ICU admissions (p [≤] 0.05). Sea-level pressure demonstrated a significant association in 29.3% of the models. Heat-related variables, including tropical nights (18.3%) and summer days (17.8%), were significantly associated with ICU admissions in Germany. Among air pollutants, ozone showed the highest proportion of significant associations (15.6%). Significant associations for heat-related atmospheric variables were observed more frequently among men and persons [≥]60 years. Mean model performance across all models was 10% WED. The models for ICU admissions due to myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) in the East German Lowlands demonstrated the best model performance (WED: 49%).  DiscussionAtmospheric factors were associated with ICU admissions, and these associations differed by region, disease, and age-sex group. Pressure- and heat-related factors were the most relevant atmospheric factors. These findings indicate that atmospheric factors have the potential to adversely impact intensive health care preparedness and delivery.

Title: Study protocol for a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial to assess chemoprotective efficacy of Aqueous standardized extract of Tinospora cordifolia (AsSET) in patients receiving Docetaxel based chemotherapy for advanced / metastatic solid tumors
Authors: GOTA, V.; Singh, P. A.; Shirsat, A.; Shetty, S.; Bhor, P.; Joshi, A.; Vaidya, A.; Rege, N.; Kumar, P.; Noronha, V.; Ramaswamy, A.; Otswal, V.; Raut, A.; Joshi, J.
Abstract: IntroductionDocetaxel is widely used for advanced and metastatic solid tumours, but dose limiting toxicities, particularly haematological adverse events, often lead to treatment delays, dose reductions or discontinuation and impair quality of life. Tinospora cordifolia (Guduchi), long used in Ayurveda for its immunomodulatory and rejuvenating properties, has shown chemoprotective potential in experimental and early clinical studies, but robust randomized evidence is lacking. This trial evaluates whether adding an aqueous standardized extract of T. cordifolia(AsSET) to docetaxel-based chemotherapy reduces grade [≥]2 adverse events and improves quality of life in patients with advanced or metastatic solid tumours.  Methods and analysisThis randomized, double-blind, and placebo-controlled trial designed to evaluate the chemoprotective efficacy of an aqueous standardised extract of Tinospora cordifolia (AsSET) in patients with advanced, recurrent or metastatic solid tumors receiving docetaxel-based chemotherapy. A total of 81 eligible patients that have provided informed consent were recruited in the study. Participants were randomized 2:1 to AsSET or placebo using stratified permuted block randomization stratified by planned cumulative docetaxel dose ([≤] 225 vs >225 mg/m2) except five participants enrolled before that date were allocated by minimization. All participants received standard intravenous docetaxel-based chemotherapy plus oral administration of either AsSET (two 300mg tablets, 600mg, twice daily) or matching placebo, from enrolment until completion of docetaxel-based therapy. Clinical, laboratory, imaging, and questionnaire based-assessment were performed at baseline, at scheduled interval during treatment and at the final visit. In consenting participants, blood samples for pharmacokinetics were collected once, at nine timepoints up to 24 hours, in any chemotherapy cycle from cycle 2 onwards. Adverse events were graded according to CTCAE version 5.0. The primary outcome is the proportion of patients experiencing grade [≥]2 adverse events from first dose to study completion (up to 24 weeks). Secondary outcomes include quality of life measured by the EORTC QLQ-C30 and the disease-site-specific FACT scale, progression-free survival (PFS) per RECIST v1.1, haematological and biochemical parameters, and pharmacokinetic parameters. The database was locked on 17 September 2026 and the locked dataset was transferred to an independent statistician who remains blinded to treatment allocation. Unblinding has not yet been done and outcome analysis has not started.  Ethics and disseminationThis study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee III (IEC) of the Advanced Centre for Treatment Research & Education in Cancer, Tata Memorial Centre, (ACTREC), Kharghar, Sector 22, Navi Mumbai (project approval no. 900950; first approved on 28 June 2023; this paper describes the most recently amended protocol, version 4.0 dated 24 February 2026; amendments are listed in Annexure 1). The trial is registered with the Clinical Trials Registry-India (CTRI/2023/08/056129) and is conducted in accordance with ICH Good Clinical Practice, the new drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019. All participants provided written informed consent, with an additional consent for pharmacokinetic sampling. Participants data are coded to protect confidentiality, and no participant will be identified in any publication without permission. The findings from this study will be presented at an academic conference and published in scholarly journals regardless of the findings.  Trial registration: CTRI/2023/08/056129  Strengths and limitation of this study{square} Robust design in the form of randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with stratified block randomization provides good internal validity {square}The study is adequately powered to demonstrate the treatment effect for the underlying assumptions {square}Pharmacokinetic sampling in a subset of participants allows assessment of whether AsSET alters docetaxel exposure, an important concern for herb-drug interactions in integrative oncology. {square}The study, being limited to docetaxel-based chemotherapy regimens at a single institution, may not be generalizable to other cytotoxic chemotherapy regimen. {square}The inclusion of patients with multiple solid tumours receiving varied docetaxel-based regimens may lead to heterogeneity in the chemotherapy-related adverse events which could affect the interpretability of pooled results. {square}The 2:1 allocation reduces statistical efficiency compared with equal allocation.

Title: Constructing expert models of adolescent vaping behaviour: A mental models study
Authors: Berg, S. H.; Stifjell, K.; Borch, K. B.; Nost, T. H.; Roislien, J.; Sandanger, T. M.
Abstract: Research on vaping prevention messages has predominantly examined adolescents perceptions of and responses and the research exploring how experts perspectives is limited. Expert knowledge is crucial for conceptualising the risk phenomenon and its key causal mechanisms, uncertainties, and issues that are relevant to address in evidence-based communication strategies. This study therefore explored how professionals and experts conceptualise and understand adolescent vaping behaviour, including its perceived causes and drivers.  Semi-structured interviews were conducted with a purposive sample of 12 experts from medical research, addiction science, public health prevention, and adolescent-oriented practice in Norway. Data collection and analysis were informed by the mental models approach to risk communication.  The analysis identified an expert-derived mental model/influence diagram of adolescent vaping behaviour. Across expert domains, vaping was understood as a multifactorial phenomenon emerging from interacting biological, psychological, and social factors operating across multiple system levels. The first theme describes vaping initiation as a socially embedded and often intermittent practice shaped by identity development, peer belonging, and low perceived harm. The second theme captures how vaping is enabled, sustained, and legitimised through interacting drivers operating across social, structural, commercial, and regulatory contexts. The third theme focuses on reinforcement processes, whereby nicotine dependence and emotional coping mechanisms contribute to more sustained use. According to these expert accounts, adolescent vaping is sustained and legitimised through broader processes of normalisation operating across multiple societal levels. The expert perspectives identified in this study suggest that comparative risk framings of e-cigarettes as less harmful than cigarettes, and the social functions of vaping within adolescent peer cultures, may be important considerations in the development of risk communication targeting adolescents.

Title: Longitudinal Associations of Cigarette Smoking, Smoking Intensity, and Smoking TrajectoriesWith Emergency Room Utilization Among U.S. Adults
Authors: Guo, W.; Yan, X.; Tatsuoka, C.
Abstract: BackgroundTobacco smoking is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the United States, yet its longitudinal association with emergency room (ER) utilization remains understudied. We examined whether cigarette smoking, smoking intensity, and smoking trajectories were associated with subsequent ER use.  MethodsWe analyzed adult respondents from Waves 1-6 of the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health Study. Wave 1-3 smoking status, intensity, and cigarettes/day were examined in relation to next-wave ER outcomes. Logistic generalized estimating equation models were used for any ER visit and frequent ER use ([≥]2 visits), and quasi-Poisson models were used for ER visit count. Trajectory analyses examined Wave 1-5 smoking patterns and Wave 6 ER outcomes, with Wave 1-4 to Wave 5 as sensitivity analysis. Marginal structural models and propensity score matching were used to strengthen causal interpretation. Models adjusted for demographics, insurance, self-rated health, and baseline ER use. Survey weights with balanced repeated replication and Fays adjustment were used.  ResultsIn adjusted GEE models, current smoking was associated with higher subsequent ER utilization, including any ER visit (OR 1.128, 95% CI [1.068-1.191]), frequent ER use (OR 1.275, 95% CI [1.185-1.372]), and ER visit count (RR 1.264, 95% CI [1.160-1.377]; all p<0.001). Smoking intensity showed a dose-response pattern: smoking <20 cigarettes/day was associated with any ER visit (OR 1.130, 95% CI [1.060-1.204]), frequent ER use (OR 1.231, 95% CI [1.124-1.347]), and ER visit count (RR 1.262, 95% CI [1.110-1.435]), while smoking[≥] 20 cigarettes/day showed stronger associations with any ER visit (OR 1.231, 95% CI [1.127-1.345]), frequent ER use (OR 1.447, 95% CI [1.293-1.618]), and ER visit count (RR 1.368, 95% CI [1.245-1.504]; all p<0.001). Each additional cigarette/day was also associated with higher ER utilization (OR/RR range, 1.007- 1.011; all p<0.001). Findings were consistent in marginal structural models and propensity score matched analyses. In trajectory analyses, new/intermittent and persistent smokers had significantly higher ER utilization, while former/intermittent smokers and sustained quitters did not differ from non-smokers, suggesting that this harmful association was eliminated by smoking cessation.  ConclusionsSmoking, heavier intensity, and persistent or emerging smoking patterns were associated with higher subsequent ER utilization, while smoking cessation reduces ER risk to the same level as non-smokers. This supports smoking prevention and cessation as strategies to reduce acute healthcare burden.  IMPLICATIONSSmoking should be considered not only a risk factor for long-term chronic disease, but also a predictor of acute healthcare utilization. The consistency of findings across longitudinal, marginal structural, and propensity score matched analyses supports a potential causal relationship between smoking exposure and subsequent emergency room use. These results strengthen the rationale for integrating smoking cessation counseling, nicotine replacement therapy, quitline referral, and preventive care linkage into emergency and urgent care settings, alongside broader tobacco-control policies to reduce acute healthcare burden.

Title: Socioeconomic Inequities in Early Kidney Care Concentrate at Late Initial Clinical Detection Rather Than Planned Care: A Population-Based Study
Authors: Cowan, E.; Rzewuska Diaz, M.; Bell, S.; Fraser, S.; Hughes, A.; Keskindag, B.; Methven, S.; Nath, M.; Nitsch, D.; Scholes-Robertson, N.; Smith, R.; Traill, P.; Blakeman, T.; Sawhney, S.
Abstract: IntroductionSocioeconomic inequities in chronic kidney disease (CKD) outcomes are recognised and greater at early stages, but where exactly inequities arise within early care remains unclear. This distinction is critical: if disparities occur before clinical recognition, strategies focused on management after diagnosis may have limited impact.  MethodsWe conducted a population-based cohort study linking healthcare and Census data for adults in North-East Scotland, 2011-2020. We examined sequential components of early kidney care from initial clinical detection (eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m{superscript 2}). Exposures were household and neighbourhood deprivation and living circumstances (rurality, living alone, mental health). Components of early kidney care were: prior surveillance; presentation (including late/unmonitored); confirmation/monitoring; treatment initiation; and unplanned emergency care. Adjusted risk ratios were estimated using modified Poisson models. Mortality was assessed up to 10 years using Cox regression with separate short-term (<1 year) and long-term estimates.  ResultsAmong 44,252 individuals, inequities were most pronounced at initial clinical detection. Individuals from deprived households were more likely to present late (adjusted RR 1.69, 95% CI 1.48-1.93). Inequities in planned monitoring after presentation were less evident (RR 1.00, 0.95- 1.05). Urine albumin testing was infrequent among those with cardiovascular risk factors. Late presentation was also associated with increased mortality (adjusted HR 1.78, 1.70-1.87), persisting beyond the first year.  ConclusionsSocioeconomic inequities in CKD are greatest at or before initial clinical detection, with late presentation a measurable indicator. Emphasis on primary care monitoring and prescribing is unlikely to reduce disparities if early detection and awareness are not also addressed.  Key messagesO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSSocioeconomic inequities in chronic kidney disease (CKD) outcomes are recognised and greater at early stages, but there is limited evidence of where these inequities arise within the early care pathway. If disparities occur before clinical detection, strategies focused on improving management of already known patients after diagnosis may have limited impact.  What this study addsDeprived populations were substantially more likely to present late, whereas differences in subsequent monitoring and treatment were small. Late presentation was strongly associated with mortality, identifying a high-risk group that reflects upstream inequities in detection and access.  How this study might affect research, practice or policyThese findings challenge strategies that focus solely on optimising monitoring and prescribing for patients already known to services. Efforts to improve CKD outcomes should prioritise earlier detection and engagement in underserved communities. Late presentation may serve as a measurable indicator of inequitable access and system performance in early kidney care.

Title: Target Trial Emulation of Metformin for Dementia Prevention in All of Us: Robustness to Cohort and Confounder Definitions
Authors: Charpignon, M.-L.; Shnitzer, T.; Iraqui, A.; Pace, D. F.; Maddah, M.; Uhler, C.
Abstract: Metformin use has been associated with a lower risk of incident dementia than other antidiabetics. We perform target trial emulation and causal competing risk analysis in the NIH All of Us (AoU) Research Program database, contrasting the effects of metformin and sulfonylurea initiation on dementia onset and death without dementia. AoU's social and behavioral health data allowed us to test robustness to excluding such confounders, and we further adjusted for calendar year effects and prior antidiabetic exposure, using both semiparametric Cox proportional hazards (PH) models and nonparametric models. Under stabilized inverse propensity score of treatment weighting, metformin was associated with a substantially lower risk of death (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.61, 95% CI: [0.49, 0.75]) and a lower incidence of dementia (HR: 0.90, 95% CI: [0.82, 1.02]). Estimated HRs were closely aligned with estimates obtained in the UK primary care and US Mass General Brigham health systems. This finding was robust to the inclusion of participants without a type 2 diabetes diagnosis at baseline and to the consideration of different covariate sets in the propensity score model, supporting metformin as a promising candidate for dementia prevention and motivating prospective validation.

Title: Association between trajectories of breastfeeding duration and infant health: Prospective cohort study
Authors: Dessy, T.; Dennis, C.-L.
Abstract: BackgroundBreastfeeding is a modifiable pathway contributing to infant health.  ObjectivesTo estimate trajectories of breastfeeding and the association between trajectories of breastfeeding and infant health.  MethodsWe conducted a prospective longitudinal cohort study (2014-2020, Canada) with 3217 cohabitating English-literate mother-father-infant triads with internet or telephone access. Women with major psychiatric conditions or suicidality were excluded. Data were collected online at baseline (<3 weeks postpartum), 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 months. Breastfeeding was measured at 0-12 months. Baseline measures included attention-deficit disorder with/without hyperactivity (ADHD, Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale) and childhood adversity (Adverse Childhood Experiences International Questionnaire). We measured infant health at 12-24 months using the Brief Infant-Toddler Social and Emotional Assessment (challenging behaviors) and self-reported number of emergent visits (>90th percentile). We estimated trajectories of breastfeeding using latent class growth analysis. Associations were estimated using adjusted linear mixed models.  ResultsMost included mothers (n=2548) were of Canadian birth (2078/2548, 82%) and graduated from university (1920/2548, 75%); few reported unemployment (222/2548, 9%) or prenatal depression (240/2548, 9%). We identified two trajectories of breastfeeding: Constant Breastfeeding (1522/2548, 60%) and Decreasing Breastfeeding (1026/2548, 40%). No statistically significant differences were observed between classes for either the risk of challenging behaviors (RR -0.006 95% CI -0.028 to 0.016) or the risk of emergent visits (RR -0.015 95% CI -0.053 to 0.023).  ConclusionsIn this study, discontinued breastfeeding was not associated with infant health. Future studies should focus on 6-month exclusive breastfeeding, a modifiable therapeutic infant feeding target.  Article SummaryIn this prospective community-based cohort of 2548 Canadian mother-father-infant triads, we observed that maternal lifetime risk factors of depression - ADHD and childhood adversity - were associated with increased risk of infant morbidity from 12-24 months, but not decreasing vs. constant breastfeeding from 0-12 months. Breastfeeding duration was not significantly associated with infant morbidity.

Title: Maternal ADHD and exclusive breastfeeding: A prospective community-based cohort study
Authors: Dessy, T.; Dennis, C.-L.
Abstract: ImportanceMaternal attention-deficit disorder with or without hyperactivity (ADHD) is an established risk factor for adverse perinatal outcomes that remains understudied to breastfeeding.  ObjectiveTo estimate the effect of maternal ADHD on 6-month exclusive breastfeeding.  DesignA prospective longitudinal community-based cohort study.  SettingCanada, 2014-2020.  ParticipantsWe included 3217 English-literate mother-father dyads with internet or telephone access, comprising women with singleton birth within 3 weeks postpartum (study baseline) and were cohabiting with the biological father. Women with major psychiatric conditions or suicidality were excluded. All participants provided informed consent at recruitment. Data were collected online through self-report questionnaires.  ExposureMaternal ADHD was measured at baseline using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (sum of scores [≥]14).  Main Outcomes and MeasuresWe defined 6-month exclusive breastfeeding based on maternal reported infant feeding, assessed at 3 and 6 months. Maternal childhood adversity (Adverse Childhood Experiences International Questionnaire, ACE-IQ; sum score) was included as a confounder. The average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) was estimated using linear probability models. We calculated 95% percentile bootstrap CI. Missing data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations with 10 iterations.  ResultsComplete-case analyses included 2071/3217 mother-father dyads, most of which were Canadian-born (79%). Childhood adversity, mental health conditions, and substance use were higher among mothers who screened positive for ADHD (4%) than among those who did not: the median number of ACE was 5 IQR 4-6; 38% self-reported prenatal depression, 13% smoked cigarettes and 19% drank alcohol during pregnancy; 11% of infants used the neonatal intensive care unit. Notably, though 90% of mothers with ADHD intended to breastfeed exclusively only 28% breastfed exclusively for 6 months. Among families with maternal ADHD, the effect of maternal ADHD on 6-month exclusive breastfeeding was ATT -0.105, 95% CI -0.209 to -0.003 in the model adjusted for maternal ACE and paternal ADHD. With multiple imputation: ATT -0.109, 95% CI -0.213 to -0.004.  Conclusions and RelevanceMothers with ADHD intend to breastfeed their infants exclusively, but additional challenges shorten the duration of exclusive breastfeeding, indicating a need for interventions tailored to neurodevelopmental differences.  KEY POINTSO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSDoes maternal ADHD influence exclusive breastfeeding duration?  FindingsIn this community-based cohort study of 3217 mother-father dyads in Canada, most mothers with ADHD intended to breastfeed exclusively, but few actually maintained it for 6 months. Maternal ADHD predicted lower probability of exclusive breastfeeding until 6 months among families with maternal ADHD.  MeaningTo equitably promote maternal and infant well-being, early detection and support for breastfeeding challenges are needed for mothers with ADHD.

Title: Culture-free Helicobacter pylori genomics reveals within-host virulence heterogeneity and antibiotic resistance
Authors: Liu, Y.; Ni, M.; Zhang, X.-S.; Bass, J.; Deshpande, P.; Romero-Gallo, J.; Chen, H.; Fan, Y.; Wang, D.; Qiao, W.; Zhang, Y.; Mead, E. A.; Dias-Neto, E.; Corvalan, A.; Brody, R.; Camargo, C. M.; Szymczak, W.; Klion, A. D.; Peek, R. M.; Blaser, M. J.; Fang, G.
Abstract: Helicobacter pylori (Hp) infects over 40% of the worlds population and causes most cases of gastric cancer worldwide, yet fundamental questions about its within-host genetic diversity remain unresolved. Decades of work on Hp genomics depends on culturing clinical isolates, which can distort within-host genetic heterogeneity that informs Hp virulence and antimicrobial resistance. Culture-free alternatives have been limited by the extremely low Hp abundance in gastric tissue (usually 10-3 to 10-7 of total genomic DNA), making direct metagenomics prohibitively expensive and existing enrichment strategies insufficient for whole-genome recovery. Here we develop ultra-sensitive Hp sequencing (uHp-seq) for reconstructing Hp genomes directly from gastric biopsies. uHp-seq achieves a thousand-fold Hp DNA enrichment and recovers near-complete genomes across samples spanning orders of magnitude in Hp abundance. Notably, individual hosts may harbor multiple co-existing Hp strains or cagA EPIYA variants with different oncogenic potential. Resistance-associated variants for six commonly used antibiotics are resolved with greater accuracy than PCR-based and probe-based commercial panels. Applied to minimally invasive gastric string samples, uHp-seq delivers reliable resistance profiles without endoscopy, opening a path to genome-guided Hp eradication.

Title: Oral rehydration salts and zinc for childhood diarrhoea in Bangladesh, 2019 and 2025: coverage, wealth inequality and reported source of care
Authors: Hoque, S. M. A. U.; Hasan, M. K.; Rahman, M. A.; Islam, M. K.; Ahmed, T.; Haque, S. M. R.; Islam, M. R.; Baset, K. u.
Abstract: BackgroundDiarrhoea remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality among children under five. WHO and UNICEF recommend oral rehydration salts (ORS) alongside 10 to 14 days of zinc supplementation. However, national progress in combined treatment coverage and its socioeconomic and care-related inequalities remains insufficiently understood in Bangladesh. We assessed combined coverage, wealth inequality and differences by reported source of care.  MethodsWe analysed children under five with caregiver-reported diarrhoea in the 2019 (n=1,589) and 2025 (n=1,634) Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS). We estimated combined coverage using design-based methods, wealth inequality using slope indices, and associations with source of care using pooled adjusted prevalence ratios (aPR). Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) estimates provided an external comparison.  ResultsCombined ORS and zinc coverage increased from 35.0% (95% CI 32.3 to 37.7) in 2019 to 42.9% (40.1 to 45.8) in 2025. In 2025, ORS and zinc coverage were 75.8% and 51.9%, respectively. The 2025 estimate agreed with DHS 2022, whereas MICS 2019 was below DHS 2017-18. Wealth inequality persisted in 2025 (slope index 13.0 percentage points, 3.4 to 22.6). Adjustment attenuated the pooled slope index from 11.8 to 6.5 points (-1.7 to 14.6). Coverage was lower with pharmacy-only than public care (aPR 0.59, 0.53 to 0.66) and with no care reported (0.14, 0.11 to 0.18). Children with no care reported accounted for 43.7% of children without combined treatment in 2025.  ConclusionsCombined coverage increased, although the apparent progress may be overstated by the lower MICS 2019 estimate relative to DHS. Zinc remained the larger treatment gap, while one in four children received no ORS. Reported sources of care require cautious interpretation.

Title: The impact of warning labels versus traffic light labels on food choice and negative emotional responses: two randomised controlled trials among UK adult populations with and without an eating disorder
Authors: Evans, R. K.; Latham, R.; Finlay, A.; Robinson, E.
Abstract: BackgroundIn the UK, front-of-pack traffic light labels (TLL) are implemented voluntarily. The UK Government are considering alternative FOP approaches, such as nutrient warning labels (WL). However, the effects and potential harm of TLL versus WL in UK consumers are unclear. We compared the effects of WL, TLL, and no label on unhealthy food item selection and negative affect among UK adults with and without an eating disorder (ED).  MethodsWe conducted two online randomised controlled trials. In Study 1, 924 UK adults without an ED diagnosis were randomly assigned (1:1:1) to a WL, TLL, or no labels condition and completed a food-choice task. In Study 2, 240 UK adults with an ED diagnosis completed a baseline no-label food choice task and were subsequently randomly assigned (1:1:1) to WL, TLL, or no labels for a follow-up food choice task. The primary outcome was the number of task-specific unhealthy food items selected. Negative affect before and after food choice tasks was measured as a secondary outcome.  FindingsIn Study 1 (data collected 02/25 - 04/25), unhealthy food selection differed by condition (p = .013). Of five products selected, WL participants selected 0.20 fewer unhealthy items than TLL participants (8.0%; p = .038) and 0.28 fewer than controls (10.7%; p = .004). In Study 2 (data collected 11/25 - 02/26), unhealthy selection decreased by 0.39 items with WL (17.7%; p = .015), 0.13 with TLL (5.3%, p = .286), and 0.00 with no labels. The reduction was greater with WL than with no labels (p = .029). Label condition did not differentially affect task-related negative affect in either study (Study 1, p = .757; Study 2, p = .448).  InterpretationWL tended to be associated with lower unhealthy food selection compared to TLL in UK adults. There was minimal evidence that WL or TLL caused negative emotional responses. Title: VaccineScout: A Computational Framework for Guiding the Composition and Valency of SARS-CoV-2 Vaccine Updates
Authors: Gangwar, P.; Khanna, S.; Wertheim, J.; Lin, B.; Turakhia, Y.
Abstract: The continual evolution of SARS-CoV-2 necessitates periodic vaccine updates to maintain immunity against newly emerging variants. However, vaccine design remains largely guided by experimental serological studies, and there is no publicly available computational framework to help systematically prioritize vaccine variants and guide valency selection. Here, we analyze over 14 million SARS-CoV-2 genomes collected globally between 2021 and 2025 and find that over half of spike amino acid sequences (primary vaccine target) observed during the first six months after vaccine selection were already circulating at the time of selection, compared with only 5-10% of sequences during the subsequent six months. These findings provide quantitative support for annual COVID-19 vaccine updates. We further show that circulating variant prevalence and open-source variant fitness predictors can both effectively rank circulating variants by their future prevalence. Motivated by these findings, we developed VaccineScout, a computational framework that recommends vaccine candidates by minimizing the average spike amino acid substitution distances to the forecasted prevalence of circulating variants. VaccineScout also helps determine vaccine valency by quantifying diminishing returns as additional variants are introduced. Retrospective analyses showed that VaccineScout-recommended candidates either matched U.S. Food and Drug Administration recommendations or had lower average spike sequence distances to future variants and higher fitness. In addition, their spike distances to future variants were comparable to an oracle selection informed by future prevalence, indicating near-optimal performance by this metric. Together, VaccineScout introduces an in silico framework for systematically prioritizing SARS-CoV-2 vaccine candidates for costly downstream experimental validation.

Title: Diagnostic accuracy of a single-reaction, pan-lineage Lassa virus RT-PCR at two Nigerian laboratories: a retrospective and prospective cohort study
Authors: Adedosu, N. A.; Alhaji, S. Y.; Etafo, J.; Abduljalail, I. I.; Aderibigbe, R. I.; Atu, A. O.; Gbenga-Ayeni, O.; Mikail, B. A.; Uzuajemeh, R. I.; Yarima, A. M.; Njoku-Attah, N.; MacLeod, I. J.
Abstract: Background Lassa virus (LASV) intra- and inter-lineage nucleotide diversity has made it challenging to develop a single-reaction RT-PCR assay that can detect all viral variants with equal sensitivity. We evaluated PANDAA(R) LASV, a single-reaction pan-lineage RT-PCR assay, at two Nigerian Lassa fever laboratories against the RealStar(R) Lassa Virus RT-PCR Kit 2.0, the current diagnostic standard in Nigeria, which requires two separate reactions per patient sample to mitigate against false negative results. Methodology and Principal Findings We conducted a diagnostic accuracy study using retrospectively (n = 200) and prospectively (n = 100) plasma samples that had been collected from patients meeting the standard case definition of suspected Lassa fever for testing by real-time PCR at Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University Teaching Hospital in Bauchi and Federal Medical Centre in Owo. PANDAA LASV(R) sensitivity was 98.6% (138/140; 95% CI 94.9-99.8%), specificity 99.4% (155/156; 96.5-100%), and accuracy 99.0% (293/296; 97.1-99.8%). The positive likelihood ratio was 153.8 (21.8-1084.9) and the negative likelihood ratio 0.01 (0.00-0.06). PANDAA Ct values correlated significantly with the reference assay L gene target (Spearman's {rho} = 0.80; p < 0.0001) and GPC target ({rho} = 0.69; p < 0.0001). Three confirmed discordant results occurred at high Ct values near assay detection limits. Performance was consistent across sites with overlapping confidence intervals for sensitivity and specificity and no difference in median Ct values for any assay target between laboratories. Ct values were significantly lower in patients [≥] 45 years (p = 0.008). Conclusions and Significance PANDAA(R) LASV demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy to detect Lassa virus RNA compared to the dual-reaction reference assay. Reducing the operational burden from two PCR reactions per sample to a single PANDAA(R) LASV reaction while maintaining equivalent sensitivity and specificity could have a direct impact on labour and reagent costs, and turnaround time. Clinical validation against additional LASV lineages is an immediate priority.

Title: Before AI tells patients what to eat, it needs to know where they live: a cross-sectional ecological study of diabetes and food access in California and Michigan census tracts, with a spotlight on Metro Detroit and Metro Los Angeles
Authors: Chitipolu, S. S.
Abstract: Background: AI chatbots now give people with diabetes diet advice, but whether those foods can be bought near home is rarely checked. Methods: In a cross-sectional ecological study of 11,974 California and Michigan census tracts, I linked diabetes prevalence (CDC PLACES 2025) with two USDA food-access maps: all SNAP-authorized stores (2025) and large grocery stores only (2019). I identified double-burden tracts (high diabetes and low income/low access) and hidden food deserts (low access to large grocery stores, but not to any SNAP store). In a pilot, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude generated meal plans for the same person across 20 high-diabetes tracts in Metro Los Angeles and Metro Detroit; I scored whether advice was healthy and whether foods were sold at nearby store types. Results: Double-burden tracts were few (71 in California, 19 in Michigan), almost none in the two metros. Food-desert tracts had a 1.5 percentage-point higher diabetes prevalence (95% CI, 1.0-2.0). Counting all SNAP stores hid 567 Californian and 329 Michigan food deserts; in Metro Detroit, all 97 disappeared, including 51 high-diabetes tracts with about 19,500 adults with diabetes. Chatbot advice was healthy, but in hidden tracts 30% of recommended foods were not reliably sold nearby; the chatbots barely adjusted. Of 55 places they named, 13% had errors, and most were over a mile away. Conclusions: The current USDA map obscures food deserts, especially in Detroit, and AI diet advice barely adjusts for them. AI nutrition tools for diabetes should include a place-aware check built on public food-access data.

Title: Estimating duration in sex work from cross-sectional studies: a Bayesian global synthesis suggests shorter durations
Authors: Knight, J.; Wang, S.; Wang, L.; Mishra, S.
Abstract: Durations selling sex are key determinants of HIV/STI transmission dynamics and service coverage. Such durations are usually estimated from cross-sectional surveys of people actively selling sex. However, cross-sectional surveys are more likely to include individuals selling sex for longer, and survey-reported durations will be right-censored. Prior works have not adequately addressed these two competing biases. In this paper, we derive the mathematical relationship between the distribution of durations reported in cross-sectional surveys and the distribution of true durations in the population overall. These distributions will be identical if true durations are exponentially distributed; otherwise, reported durations will typically underestimate the variance in true durations. We develop a parametric Bayesian model of this relationship, and apply it to re-analyze aggregate data from a global systematic review. Our model-estimated average true durations selling sex are significantly shorter than previously published for all regions - e.g. in Africa: 2.1 (95% CI: 1.8-2.5) versus 5.5 years; in Asia: 1.4 (1.2-1.5) versus 2.8-4.0 years. Shorter average durations then suggest that HIV incidence in sex work could be higher than previously thought, to match the same HIV prevalence data. Our approach can be applied beyond sex work, to characterize duration distributions for any transient risk/disease state.

Title: The evolving epidemiology of scrub typhus in Thailand (2003-2024): insights from latent process modelling of national surveillance data
Authors: Wongnak, P.; Chaisiri, K.; Perrone, C.; Chalvet-Monfray, K.; Areechokchai, D.; Pan-ngum, W.
Abstract: Background: Scrub typhus is a major yet neglected vector-borne disease in Thailand, where it has been nationally notifiable for over two decades. However, long-term changes in its epidemiology, including reporting proportions, transmission intensity, disease severity, and seasonal patterns, have not been comprehensively characterised at the national level. Methodology: We analysed 22 years of national surveillance data for scrub typhus in Thailand (2003-2024) using a latent process model that jointly fits reported cases with published nationwide seroprevalence data and antibody kinetics to estimate reporting proportions and underlying transmission dynamics across all 77 provinces of Thailand. Findings: Over the 22-year study period, 143096 cases and 119 deaths were reported nationally. Estimated reporting proportion broadly mirrored transmission intensity, being higher in high-burden regions and lower elsewhere. Estimated reporting proportion declined synchronously across all regions during the COVID-19 pandemic, followed by rapid rebound by 2024. After adjusting for estimated reporting, the estimated force of infection was highest in the northern provinces but also substantial in the northeast and south, with upward trends in some provinces. Susceptibility among older adults aged 65 and above increased progressively over the study period, reversing the pattern observed two decades earlier. Case-fatality among reported cases in the 25-35-year reference group was low and declined from 0.15% (95% Credible Interval [CrI]: 0.07-0.30%) to 0.06% (95% CrI: 0.02-0.12%), while relative case-fatality among adults above 65 remained elevated across all periods. Three seasonal patterns, differing mainly in peak timing, were identified and remained largely stable over time. Conclusion: Over two decades, scrub typhus transmission in Thailand appears to extend well beyond its traditionally recognised northern focus, with estimated substantial burden in regions that have received less attention, while the demographic profile of those most affected has shifted progressively toward older adults. These findings support the need for regionally tailored surveillance, age-targeted clinical preparedness, and sustained investment in understanding the ecological drivers of transmission.

Title: Place-based structural disadvantage and mortality inequality across 379 Polish counties, 2010-2025: a spatial Mundlak analysis
Authors: Madej, T.; Wojtyniak, B.; Rabczenko, D.; Smaga, A.; Boguslawski, S.
Abstract: Place-based mortality inequalities may persist even as short-term associations with local conditions change. We examined age-sex-standardised all-cause mortality in 379 harmonised Polish counties (2010-2025), asking whether durable between-county differences or lagged within-county deviations better characterise mortality geography. Spatial Mundlak generalised additive models allowed non-linear associations and county-specific spatial modification; a pre-COVID model (2010-2019) was compared with overlapping models through 2022 and 2025. In the pre-COVID model, median county average partial slopes per standard deviation were -26.1 deaths per 100,000 for higher education, +29.4 for primary/lower-secondary education and +30.2 for PM2.5. Directions of these between-county gradients persisted across analytical windows. By contrast, within-county associations were less stable and sometimes reversed sign in pandemic-inclusive models. County-level uncertainty indicated stronger and more coherent pre-COVID spatial patterns for education, PM2.5 and population density than for several health-care and migration terms. Strict leave-one-year-out validation revealed weak temporal transportability, particularly for the 2010-2022 model, limiting predictive interpretation. Outcome-defined comparisons further showed that educational composition remained an important separator of high- and low-mortality counties after COVID-19, while the fitted PM2.5 contribution contrast diminished. These findings distinguish durable configurations of place-based disadvantage from period-dependent ecological co-movement. They support geographically sensitive, multi-domain approaches to reducing mortality inequalities, while not establishing individual-level causal effects.

Title: Genotypic infection endpoint analysis to understand efficacy and escape potential of the malaria monoclonal antibody CIS43LS
Authors: Schwabl, P.; Niangaly, A.; Nickols, W.; Callier, V.; Mateja, A.; Kayentao, K.; Ongoiba, A.; Skinner, J.; Preston, A. C.; Doumbo, S.; Doumtabe, D.; Amaya-Romero, J. E.; Kelley, K. K.; Li, S.; Laws, M.; Peterson, M. E.; Tran, T. M.; Murphy, S. C.; Traore, B.; Seder, R. A.; Crompton, P. D.; Potter, G. E.; Neafsey, D. E.
Abstract: Early-phase trials of candidate malaria interventions in endemic areas often use "time-to-first" infection as a primary efficacy endpoint. This approach does not assess infection risk after the initial infection, and its censoring of trial participants after their first infection can introduce bias by removing more high-risk participants from control than treatment arms over time. Efficacy estimate precision may also decline as risk set size decreases. Here we assessed the utility of genotyping all infections in an intervention trial to determine the total infection incidence in each participant for the full follow-up period. Specifically, we genotyped all Plasmodium falciparum infections detected in a previously-reported phase 2 trial of the antimalarial monoclonal antibody CIS43LS in 330 Malian adults. We determined the molecular force of infection (molFOI; rate of new P. falciparum strains) for each participant, expressing efficacy as the percent molFOI reduction in CIS43LS versus placebo arms (EffmolFOI). Six-month EffmolFOI was 86.5% (95% CI: 80.1-90.8) and 70.7% (61.0-78.0) for the 40 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg doses, respectively. These estimates are similar to those from time-to-first infection analysis, but more precise when analyzing efficacy by trial-month and when stratifying by P. falciparum infection-status at enrollment. Participants infected at enrollment had lower EffmolFOI and acquired infections earlier in the trial, creating systematic differences in risk composition between arms over time. Genotyping showed no evidence for escape-polymorphisms in the CIS43LS epitope. These results demonstrate how genotypic endpoints can provide a more comprehensive understanding of candidate malaria interventions.

Title: Can dental EHR data support a learning health system? Completeness, consistency, and accuracy of structured versus narrative diagnoses
Authors: Chuang, Y.-S.; Lin, G.-H.; Lee, C.-T.; Brandon, R.; Walji, M. F.; Jiang, X.; Tokede, B.
Abstract: Introduction Electronic health record (EHR) data increasingly drive quality monitoring and research, yet their reliability in dentistry is uncertain. We compared the completeness, consistency, and accuracy of periodontal diagnoses captured in two different formats (structured fields versus narrative notes) across two academic dental centers sharing the same EHR platform and diagnostic terminology. Methods In this retrospective study of qualifying periodontal encounters (2021), structured diagnoses were extracted by SQL and narrative diagnoses by a fine-tuned RoBERTa NLP model. A random sample (~20%) was independently reviewed by two board-certified periodontists, with disagreements resolved by consensus, to form the gold standard. Outcomes were completeness (presence of a diagnosis), consistency (agreement between formats), and accuracy (agreement with the gold standard), with ordinal periodontal stage compared using quadratic weighted {kappa}. Results Across 4,542 encounters, completeness varied widely by site and format (34.7% - 84.5%), and neither format was consistently more complete; at one site, over one-third of encounters (35.8%) had no documented diagnosis in either format. Among dual-documented encounters, agreement between formats was substantial but imperfect ({kappa} = 0.86 and 0.80). Accuracy against the gold standard was modest for both sources (all near 50%), with narrative notes numerically higher at both sites and favored by the severity-weighted {kappa}, though raw differences were not significant. Pooled across sites, the formats diverged in 14.8% of dual-documented encounters, 8.4% by two or more stages, with the structured field carrying the milder stage in 67.9% of disagreements. Conclusions Structured and unstructured periodontal diagnoses each matched expert adjudication only about half the time, and neither was consistently more complete. Narrative notes held a small severity-weighted accuracy advantage, and coded fields more often carried the milder stage when the two disagreed. These convergent, cross-site patterns appear systematic rather than site-specific and expose latent risks for analytics and decision support. Improving dental EHR data quality will require workflows that combine the computability of coded entries with the fidelity of free text.

Title: Most coronial recommendations in Australia have no published response: a national analysis of findings and agency responses
Authors: Farquhar, H. L.
Abstract: Background: A coroner's recommendation prevents deaths only if someone acts on it. We measured how often Australian coronial recommendations receive a published response and what it says. Methods: Cross-sectional analysis of every finding and agency response in the AustLII Coronial Law Library (eight jurisdictions; enumerated February 2026). Responses were linked to findings and classified by a large language model, validated against the author's blinded coding (seven-category kappa 0.81, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.90). Response rates were measured over all years and within each jurisdiction's response-database years. Acceptance was modelled by Firth penalised logistic regression. Results: Of 9,831 findings, 4,480 (45.6%) contained recommendations. Only 1,309 of these (29.2%) had a published agency response. Within the database years the figure was 36.6% (35.0% to 38.3%), from 58.6% in Western Australia to 5.8% in Tasmania; the Australian Capital Territory has no response database. Of 1,541 findings with a classifiable response, 1,316 (85.4%; 83.5% to 87.1%) accepted the recommendations, from 65.0% in Western Australia to all 22 in the Northern Territory. Findings that mentioned a psychiatric unit (adjusted odds ratio (OR) 2.02, 1.25 to 3.35) or a prison (1.78, 1.12 to 2.92) were more likely to receive an accepting response. A mention of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander identity was not (0.78, 0.46 to 1.37). Conclusions: Most coronial recommendations in Australia have no response that anyone can find, and those that are answered in public are mostly accepted. A national register linking each recommendation to its response would make implementation, not only stated intent, possible to follow up.

Title: From district to community: expanded eligibility, not wider geography, drives schistosomiasis programme costs under revised WHO guidance in Ethiopia and Zimbabwe
Authors: Carlin, A.; Fantaguzzi, C.; Seife, F.; Leta, G. T.; Phiri, I.; Dhanani, N.; Midzi, N.; Fleming, F.
Abstract: Background Schistosomiasis remains a major public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa. Recent World Health Organization (WHO) guidance calls for community-wide treatment and fine-scale data to optimise preventive chemotherapy (PC) strategies, yet the practical implications for resource allocation by health ministries are unclear. Methods We analysed epidemiological and cost data from Ethiopia and Zimbabwe to compare survey designs and five implementation scenarios. Scenarios varied by data source, administrative unit of implementation, and WHO guidance on PC strategies. Outcomes were target population, praziquantel requirements, and delivery costs. Results The geostatistical approach reduced sample size by up to 90% and survey costs by [≥]72% compared with a design-based approach, while increasing spatial coverage. Applying updated WHO guidance expanded eligibility to pre-school-aged children and adults, and in one scenario increased treatment eligibility by 72% in Ethiopia and 262% in Zimbabwe. Correspondingly, praziquantel requirements and delivery costs were driven primarily by expanded age eligibility rather than geographic coverage. Conclusions The geostatistical approach provides substantial efficiency gains for impact assessments, enabling cost-efficient, granular targeting. However, implementing 2022 WHO guidance was the dominant driver of increases in programme scope and resource needs, underscoring the importance of accurate fine-scale data to guide efficient planning and budgeting toward elimination goals.

Title: Multidimensional deprivation and brain health in older adults in rural northern Tanzania: a cross-sectional community-based study
Authors: Folorunsho, S.; Woods, A.; Kisoli, A.; Anderson, G. S.; Mkubila, A.; Niechcial, M.; Nye, C.; Rite, S. M.; Malya, A. D.; Mtenga, S. L.; Ulomi, H. R.; Mbowe, E. N.; Mlaki, D. A.; Boshe, J.; Safic, S.; Humble, H.; Healy, C.; Fotheringham, L.; Robinson, L.; Walker, R.; Mbwele, B.; Kalaria, R.; Paddick, S.-M.
Abstract: Introduction: Dementia and late-life depression are rising rapidly in sub-Saharan Africa, yet prevention frameworks remain focused on individual behaviour. Multidimensional poverty is a plausible structural determinant of brain health but is rarely assessed. Methods: This cross-sectional analysis of the community-based Akili Mali study assessed adults aged 60 years and older in three rural communities in Kilimanjaro, Tanzania. Outcomes were the 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15), IDEA cognitive screen, CERAD ten-word list, and verbal fluency. Deprivation was measured with a nine-indicator Alkire-Foster Multidimensional Deprivation Index. Missing data were multiply imputed; models adjusted for age, sex, education, community, comorbidity, and health behaviours. Results: Of 1054 participants (mean age 70.2 years [SD 9.35]; 629 [59.7%] women), 840 (81.9%) of 1026 were multidimensionally deprived. Each unit increase in deprivation score predicted a higher GDS-15 score ({beta} 4.83, 95% CI 3.82 to 5.83), higher odds of screen-positive depression (odds ratio 17.18, 6.89 to 42.83), lower IDEA score ({beta} -1.97, -2.97 to -0.97), and lower verbal fluency ({beta} -2.57, -3.77 to -1.36; all p<0.001). CERAD measures and self-reported impairment showed no association. At community level this gradient inverted: the most deprived community had the lowest depression and highest cognition, yet perceived social standing did not differ. Conclusion: Multidimensional deprivation was near-universal and independently associated with worse brain health. The community-level inversion, with perceived social standing equivalent across communities of unequal material circumstances, indicates that absolute deprivation alone does not explain the distribution of brain health. Relative position and community resilience are priorities for study

Title: Effect of results-based financing on selected maternal and child health indicators in Mayuge District, Uganda: a comparative interrupted time series analysis
Authors: Eboga, H.; Lubaale, Y.; Oguttu, F.; Nantale, R.; Tsekpetse, P.; Makoko, B. T.; Kawala, E.; Mugahi, R.; Kazibwe, A.; Okia, D.; Musaba, M. W.; Kibuule, D.; Mukunya, D.
Abstract: Background Uganda continues to experience a high burden of maternal and child morbidity and mortality, partly due to suboptimal utilization and quality of reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health services. To address these challenges, the Ministry of Health of Uganda, with World Bank funding, implemented results-based financing (RBF) through the Uganda Reproductive, Maternal, and Child Health Services Improvement Project (URMCHIP) in selected districts. Although RBF has been implemented for nearly a decade, evidence on its impact on maternal and child health service indicators in Uganda remains limited. This study assessed the effect of RBF on selected maternal and child health indicators in Mayuge District, Uganda. Methods We retrospectively reviewed the records between July 2018 and June 2019 as the pre-intervention period, July 2019 to June 2021 as the intervention period, and July 2021 to June 2023 as the post-intervention period. We conducted multiple-group interrupted time-series analyses to compare trends in selected maternal and child health indicators between four intervention and three non-intervention health facilities. Results After the implementation of RBF, the number of births in the intervention facilities increased by 1.67 births per month (95% CI [0.19, 3.16]) as compared to the control facilities. The number of women receiving modern family planning methods in intervention facilities increased by 34.1 women per month (CI [25.8, 42.4] as compared to the control facilities. The number of children under five years seen at the outpatient department slightly decreased by -0.24 children per month (CI [-9.58, 9.10]). There was a decline in facility-based births and the number of clients receiving modern family planning methods following the discontinuation of results-based financing in the intervention health facilities. Conclusions There was an improvement in selected maternal and child health indicators in the intervention health facilities following the implementation of RBF, with a subsequent decline in facility-based births and the number of clients receiving modern family planning methods after RBF was discontinued. We recommend that policymakers consider allocating additional funds towards RBF to improve health service delivery.

Title: Clinical Evaluation of the PANDAA LASV RT-PCR Assay in Sierra Leone
Authors: Grant, D. S.; Thompson, C. R.; Sandi, J.; Manjia, M.; Kallon, T.; Kamara, M. S.; Fofanah, I.; Edwards, T. R.; Fletcher, T. E.; Byrne, R. L.
Abstract: Molecular diagnosis of Lassa fever is complicated by extensive Lassa virus genetic diversity and limited laboratory capacity in endemic settings. The RealStar(R) Lassa Virus RT-PCR Kit 2.0 is a commonly used commercial dual-target assay for LASV detection, but its two-target format requires separate amplification reactions, increasing reagent use and workflow complexity. We present the diagnostic evaluation of the single-reaction, adaptive PANDAA Lassa Virus RT-PCR assay with the dual-target RealStar(R) Lassa Virus RT-PCR Kit 2.0 using 94 archived serum samples from Sierra Leone. 79 of these samples had valid paired results, and we report a positive percent agreement of 78.12% (95% CI 61.25%-88.98%), negative percent agreement of 93.62% (95% CI 82.84%-97.81%), and an overall agreement of 87.34% (95% CI 78.24%-92.98%); Cohen {kappa} was 0.73 (95% CI 0.58-0.89). PANDAA showed substantial agreement and offers a potentially efficient single-well format, but further optimisation and prospective evaluation are needed.

Title: Building a community-academic partnership in public housing: Lessons from applying the CBPR Partnership Readiness Model
Authors: Sesay, N. A.; OoNorasak, K.; Brewer, J. E.; Bawa, M. S.; Mason, D.; Hughes, K.; Coffie, J.; White, B. M.
Abstract: The DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) eating plan has been shown to reduce hypertension; however, adherence is low among low-income African American (AA) women, who experience a disproportionate burden of hypertension. To better understand barriers to DASH among low-income AA women, specifically AA women living in public housing, we established a community-academic partnership using a project advisory board (PAB). This paper applies the CBPR Partnership Readiness Model to assess community stakeholder readiness for the partnership. PAB members were recruited through ongoing research and volunteer work in the target community. We developed a 33-page PAB workbook clarifying study goals, member roles and expectations, and hypertension information. A questionnaire was used to gather feedback on members' experiences. PAB membership increased by 150% after the first year following a second recruitment phase. Members reported satisfaction with progress toward local food equity initiatives and with partnership sustainability. Findings indicate the model was helpful in evaluating the PAB formation process for a project involving public housing stakeholders. PABs can help build local support for community-engaged projects. When members can see the advantages of their involvement, partnerships are strengthened.

Title: Demographic and economic characteristics of residents of four subsidized housing facilities in Nashville, TN, and their preferences for co-located services
Authors: Clouse, K.; Kimpel, C.; Chavez, L.; Terrell, T.; Landivar Donato, J.; Hasbrooke, N.; Frenia, M.; Elrod, B.; Ketel, C.
Abstract: Introduction: Subsidized housing provides affordable rent to low-income households, many of whom have high rates of disability and chronic disease, but it is generally not designed to deliver the health and social services these residents may need. In this study, we sought to characterize residents of four subsidized housing facilities in Nashville, Tennessee, an area marked by rapid growth, poverty, and housing instability, and to assess their preferences for co-located services. Methods: A cross-sectional study (2023-2025) recruited 140 residents from four subsidized housing facilities using randomized selection. We administered semi-structured questionnaires assessing demographics, past experiences with homelessness and incarceration, health, and preferences for health and social services. Results: Most residents were Black/African American (63.6%) and older adults, with 80% earning [≤]$20,000 annually. Most had experienced homelessness (70.0%) and over half incarceration (53.6%). Residents expressed strong interest in on-site services, particularly dental and vision care (over 90%) and adult primary care accepting TennCare/Medicaid (91.4%). Discussion: Findings depict a population facing multiple vulnerabilities, including economic instability, social isolation, and histories of homelessness and incarceration. This study highlights the importance of combining housing with comprehensive health and social services in addressing inequities and prioritizing resident feedback in service design.

Title: Investigating Climate-Driven Disruption of Malaria Transmission Following the 2022 Sindh, Pakistan Floods: An Interrupted Time Series Study
Authors: Tariq, A.; Allana, R.; Shah, S.; Kazi, A. M.; LaBeaud, A. D.
Abstract: Malaria remains a major global public health challenge in developing countries, with climate change intensifying its impact, particularly in vulnerable populations. Rising temperatures can expand the geographic range and local abundance of malaria vectors, Anopheles mosquitoes, which thrive in warm climates, with 25C representing the optimal temperature for malaria transmission. In Pakistan, malaria is primarily spread through P. falciparum and P. vivax. Pakistan is one of the seven countries in the Eastern Mediterranean Region that accounts for 98% of the total malaria burden in the region. Recently, after catastrophic flooding in Pakistan in 2022 and the subsequent increase in malaria incidence, it has become imperative to estimate the climate change-attributed increase in the risk of malaria. In this study, we analyze the time series malaria case incidence data from the province of Sindh, Pakistan, and the climate data to quantify climate-attributed malaria cases in Sindh, Pakistan. We fit a negative binomial generalized linear model (GLM) to monthly case counts with interrupted time series and seasonality terms. The majority of malaria-confirmed infections were Plasmodium Vivax (40-95%) between 2016-2024, followed by Plasmodium falciparum infections. The positivity rate for malaria remained <10% until June 2022, and increased massively after the July 2022 flooding. After accounting for this case momentum, the onset of the 2022 floods was associated with an immediate, independent increase in malaria cases of approximately threefold (IRR 2.985, 95% CI 1.878-4.751, p < 0.001). These findings suggest that post-flooding malaria surveillance and response in flood-affected settings should anticipate not only an acute environmentally driven surge in cases but also a subsequent period of elevated, self-sustaining transmission that may persist well beyond the resolution of the initiating environmental disruption, in this case the flooding.

Title: Acceptability and feasibility of measles vaccination, small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplementation, and their co-delivery among children aged 6-23 months in northern Nigeria: a qualitative study
Authors: Ahmad, S. I.; Nabunje, J.; Adamu, S. K.; Sheriff, A. M.; Gwayo, A. G.; Goje, A.; Atanga, I.; Akinyi, A. M.; Ugonna, E. C.; Bahonon, S.; Chiroma, U.; Adam, H. M.; Becquet, R.; Muhammad, N. S.; Goni, B. W.; Cazes, C.; Phelan, K. P. Q.; Plazy, M.
Abstract: Background. Undernutrition and infectious diseases form a vicious cycle that endangers child survival in low-resource settings, including in Northern Nigeria. The NutriVax-Measles trial was designed to evaluate a strategy combining preventive small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) distributions with community mobilization and routine immunization services for children aged 6-23 months to improve measles vaccination uptake. To inform future programs co-delivering nutrition supplementation and immunization services at scale, we aimed to assess the feasibility and acceptability of measles vaccination, SQ-LNS distribution, and the NutriVax strategy. Methods. A qualitative study was conducted at the end of the trial using in-depth interviews (n=53) and focus group discussions (n=8) with key stakeholders: caregivers, health care workers, community health workers, and community representatives. Thematic analysis was guided by multiple conceptual frameworks. Results. The majority of the participants expressed satisfaction with measles vaccines in both arms, and with SQ-LNS in the NutriVax arm, as they perceived the benefits for their children health. In both arms, community awareness sessions and previous experience of outbreaks were key to motivating caregivers to bring their children to healthcare centres. Although distance to health facilities was identified as one of the main barriers to accessing care, SQ-LNS was perceived as an important source of motivation to bring their child to the clinic where they subsequently received vaccination. All stakeholder groups emphasized the importance of community leaders support and targeted male sensitization to address the prevailing sociocultural norms. Additionally, improved service organization to reduce waiting time was considered crucial to enhance caregivers acceptability of the intervention. Conclusion. Both measles vaccination and SQ-LNS provision were acceptable and feasible, supporting the NutriVax strategy within primary healthcare settings in fragile health systems. Successful implementation depends on sustained community sensitization, continued engagement of fathers and community leaders, and service delivery decentralized as close as possible to beneficiaries.

Title: On conducting diary-based social contact surveys to inform transmission models of close-contact infections: a systematic review and expert-informed questionnaire
Authors: Loedy, N.; Lumia, G.; Di Domenico, L.; Suer, J.; Jit, M.; Melegaro, A.; Funk, S.; Backer, J. A.; Grijalva, C. G.; Paolotti, D.; Verbiest, J.; Ratmann, O.; Coletti, P.; Dan, S.; Colizza, V.; Beutels, P.; Willem, L.; Abrams, S.; Hens, N.
Abstract: Background: Diary-based social contact surveys are widely used to parameterise transmission models of close-contact infections. However, variation in study design, contact definitions, and questionnaire content limits comparability across studies. These challenges became particularly evident during the COVID-19 pandemic, when rapid and repeated data collection was urgently needed, often without harmonised instruments. To address these challenges, we aimed to develop an expert-informed questionnaire and update the recommendations on conducting diary-based social contact studies previously proposed by Hoang et al. (2019). Methods and findings: We conducted a systematic review of diary-based social contact surveys published between 31 January 2018 and 25 September 2025 using PubMed and the Web of Science Core Collection, extracting information on study design, survey methodology, contact definitions, and survey items from available questionnaires. Methodological quality and reporting were assessed using an adapted AXIS tool, with results summarised for each criterion. In total, we identified 129 studies across 62 countries, with most studies conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic (59.7% in 2021-2022). Retrospective reporting (86.0%) and non-probability sampling (77.5%) were largely adopted and became increasingly common during the pandemic, while non-paper-based data collection rose sharply from 2021 onwards. Across 36 retrievable questionnaires from general-population surveys, we identified 54 survey items. An online assessment involving 26 experts informed the classification of these items according to their perceived importance, resulting in an expert-informed questionnaire comprising 22 core items. Based on our findings, we updated previous recommendations on sampling, survey methods, contact definitions, behavioural change, essential contact information, and data governance. Conclusions: This study provides an expert-informed questionnaire and updated recommendations to support harmonised social contact data collection, improve comparability across studies, and strengthen preparedness for future public health emergencies.

Title: Stressful life events recorded in 39.7 million clinical notes: associations with mental disorders, comorbidity, and frailty
Authors: Peltola, A. A.; Khan, E.; Kaijansinkko, J.; Alexander, N.; Tirkkonen, A.; von Bonsdorff, M. B.; Lin, J.; Jylhava, J.
Abstract: Abstract Background: Despite being harmful to both mental and physical health, stressful life events are not recorded in structured electronic health records. They appear sporadically in narrative clinical notes, where they are difficult to analyze at scale. Natural language processing (NLP) has made clinical notes more available for research, but applications to stressful life events remain limited, leaving their documentation patterns and prognostic value understudied. By applying NLP, we identified stressful life events from clinical notes and examined their associations with mental disorders, comorbidity, and frailty. Methods: We analyzed 39.7 million clinical notes, recorded between 2010 and 2023, from 202,988 patients in Central Finland Wellbeing Services County. NLP was applied to identify stressful life events in five categories: grief, divorce, financial distress, violence, and family problems. Associations with the risk of mental disorders (stress-related disorders, anxiety, and depression) were estimated using time-varying Cox proportional hazards models, and associations with physical health outcomes (comorbidity and frailty) using generalized linear mixed models. Results: Stressful life events were identified from clinical notes with high accuracy (F1 scores 0.81-0.95). Event prevalences ranged from 0.5% for family problems to 22.1% for grief. Most individual events were associated with mental disorders, comorbidity, and frailty. The number of different life events was associated with a higher risk of stress-related (hazard ratio [HR], 1.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.58-1.67), anxiety (HR, 2.08; 95% CI, 2.03-2.14), and depressive disorders (HR, 1.99; 95% CI, 1.94-2.03), and with higher comorbidity (rate ratio, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.56-1.59) and frailty (mean ratio, 1.57; 95% CI, 1.56-1.58). Conclusions: Stressful life events were accurately identified from clinical notes and were associated with a higher risk of mental disorders, comorbidity, and frailty. Even so, violence and financial distress, the two events with comparable national estimates, were documented substantially less often than those estimates, suggesting underrecording of stressful life events in clinical settings.
